name: Dark Purple
lede: Dark Purple is the purple that nearly passes for black, the color Roman writers prized in the best shellfish dye and medieval dyers rebuilt with madder over blue.

sections.title: Plain words for a deep color
sections.body: The name is descriptive, not traditional. Our library takes the swatch from the xkcd survey and Wikipedia, and lists Deep Purple Wine, ISCC-NBS block 225, as a related name [1]. Paterson's dictionary has several single words for the idea: petunia is a dark purple, prune is the very dark purple of the plum and was popular in the 1930s, and damascene is the dark purple of the damson [2]. Compare [[purple]], [[petunia]] and [[plum]].

sections.title: A purple that looked black
sections.body: Greenfield reports that Pliny described a blend of scarlet and purple-black dyes as the color of clotted blood, blackish at first glance but gleaming in the light [3]. Dark purples were in the ascendant, yet scarlet and crimson stayed prestigious in Rome [3]. St Clair describes how the shellfish liquid turned in sunlight from pale yellow to sea green, then blue, then a dark purple-red, and the best color, tinged with blackness, came from mixing the fluids of two kinds of shellfish [4]. See [[tyrian-purple]].

sections.title: Purple from blue and red
sections.body: Medieval dyers, Pastoureau explains, gave undyed cloth a solid blue foot, then dipped it in a vat of red, madder or orchil, to get dark purples [5]. These purples were more red than blue and recalled the ancient ones [5]. The red was [[madder]].

sections.title: Minerals and pigments
sections.body: Antozonite is a dark purple to purple-black fluorite, found in Bavaria, in France and at Joachimsthal in the Czech lands [6]. In 1794 a British patent by Atkinson covered synthetic iron-oxide pigments that included a dark purple-brown [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, only 24 (0.1%) hold this swatch within six units of ΔE2000 over at least five per cent of the canvas, as photographed [8]. In all of them it plays the shadow role, the darkest part of the palette [8]. Four of the six strongest matches are portraits, led by Paggi's *Portrait of Piero di Lorenzo de' Medici*, 1586, where it covers 69% of the picture [8].

The earliest match is Ambrogio Lorenzetti's *Presentation at the Temple*, 1342 [8]. Italy has 6 matches in 1,986 paintings and France 6 in 3,443 [8]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test.
